name: Green tea (Camellia sinensis) leaf extract
lead: Green tea leaf extract is a concentrate of polyphenols, mainly catechins such as epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), from unoxidized Camellia sinensis leaves. People use it in two ways for their looks: in creams and serums, where it is included as an antioxidant to help protect skin from the oxidative stress of UV exposure that drives visible ageing, and as an oral supplement, often alongside other ingredients in leanness and general-health stacks.[1][4]

A 2022 review of its phytochemistry and pharmacology lists antioxidant, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activities, and notes it may assist treatment of dermatitis.[2] A 2015 review of herbal creams loaded with phyto-extracts, Camellia sinensis among them, summarises in vivo antioxidant studies and describes such formulations as possible cosmeceuticals for protecting skin against UV damage.[3]

Regulators and reviewers take a cautious view of oral extracts: Wikipedia reports that a 2011 European Food Safety Authority review found most proposed claims, including some on UV skin protection, not sufficiently supported, and that extracts have been associated with liver toxicity, leading Health Canada to recommend warning labels in 2017.[1]

paras: Green tea is unfermented tea that keeps much of the natural content of fresh leaves. Its main polyphenols are four catechins: epicatechin, epicatechin gallate, epigallocatechin and EGCG, the most abundant and active.[5] Other constituents include alkaloids, amino acids and polysaccharides.[2] Brewed tea is mostly water, while supplement extracts can contain up to about 17% caffeine by weight.[1]
Matcha, a shade-grown powdered green tea, is described in a review as the most concentrated source of catechins, along with theanine and chlorophyll.[5]

EGCG is an ester of epigallocatechin and gallic acid; dried green tea leaf holds about 7,380 mg per 100 g, compared with about 4,245 mg for white tea and 936 mg for black tea, where fermentation converts most catechins into theaflavins and thearubigins [19]. A cup of green tea contains roughly 165 mg of EGCG [19].

The cosmetic rationale rests on antioxidant activity: ultraviolet light produces reactive oxygen species in skin, and polyphenols are described as able to neutralise them in laboratory work [3]. Oral absorption of EGCG is described as poor, with blood levels peaking about 1.7 hours after intake and a plasma half-life near 5 hours, and methylated metabolites persisting at higher levels than unchanged EGCG [19]. Researchers note that laboratory antioxidant effects do not necessarily translate to oral intake for this reason [19].

Green tea comes from the leaves and buds of Camellia sinensis that are not oxidized, in contrast to oolong and black teas. It originated in China, spread across East Asia, and China supplied roughly 80 percent of the global green tea market as of 2015 [1]. Brewed tea is about 99.9 percent water, with caffeine and polyphenols such as EGCG as its notable constituents [1].

Concentrated extracts came later. Capsule and tablet extracts are sold as dietary supplements and can contain up to about 17 percent caffeine by weight, though decaffeinated versions exist [1]. In 2006 the US FDA approved sinecatechins, a defined water extract of green tea leaves sold as Veregen and Polyphenon E and made of mostly catechins, about 55 percent of it EGCG, as an ointment for external genital and perianal warts; it was the first botanical drug the agency approved [11]. That ointment is the main prescription use of a green tea extract applied to skin.

Green tea is made from leaves and buds of Camellia sinensis that are not withered or oxidized, unlike oolong and black teas. It originated in China in the late first millennium BC, with legendary origins attributed to Emperor Shennong [1]. Lu Yu's The Classic of Tea (618-907 AD) is regarded as a key early text, and the monk Eisai's Kissa Yojoki of 1211 discusses tea and health [1]. Tea seeds reached Japan in the early ninth century through the monks Saicho and Kukai; Japanese tea is typically steamed, producing a sweeter, grassier taste, and matcha is shade-grown, ground tea used in the tea ceremony [1]. China supplied about 80 percent of the global green tea market in 2015 [1].

Supplement-style extracts are a modern development of this beverage. Capsule and tablet extracts can contain up to about 17 percent caffeine by weight [1]. The US FDA issued several warning letters to green tea extract makers between 2008 and 2017, most citing disease treatment or prevention claims that legally classed products as unapproved drugs [19].

In cosmetics, green tea extract is promoted as an antioxidant and soothing ingredient. Reviews of plant-extract creams include Camellia sinensis among botanicals studied to quench reactive oxygen species produced by UV exposure, which contributes to skin ageing.[3]

Oral green tea extract appears in supplement stacks discussed on T Nation by lifters, listed alongside fish oil, vitamins and fat-loss ingredients.[6][7] A 2022 review also reports potential use as an aid in dermatitis.[2]

In skincare, green tea extract and its catechins are included for their antioxidant and soothing character. The rationale is that ultraviolet exposure generates reactive oxygen species that contribute to visible ageing, and that polyphenols can quench them; a 2015 review of herbal creams lists Camellia sinensis among the botanicals studied for this purpose in laboratory and in vivo antioxidant experiments [3]. A 2022 review summarises antioxidant, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activity and mentions use as an aid in dermatitis [2].

Regulators have commented on the topical claims. Wikipedia reports that the European Food Safety Authority's 2011 review found most proposed green tea health claims, including claims about protection against UV-related skin damage, not sufficiently supported [1]. The NIH's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, for its part, mentions only the prescription wart ointment in connection with the skin [13].

Green tea extract capsules are used in lean-physique and general-health stacks. The NCCIH states that the catechins and caffeine in green tea may have a modest effect on body weight, depending on product makeup and the person's activity level, and notes that weight-loss products often combine green tea with other ingredients [13]. Wikipedia's summary of the clinical literature reports no good evidence of weight loss from green tea [1]. T Nation forum threads list green tea extract among supplements used by lifters alongside fish oil and other products [6][7].
A randomized trial in untrained men examined a Camellia sinensis polyphenol blend for 28 days around resistance exercise and measured muscle apoptotic signalling rather than appearance [9].

Excess consumption, especially of extracts, has been associated with liver toxicity and rarely liver failure; the 2022 review also raises hepatotoxicity and DNA damage concerns for extracts and main ingredients [1][2]. The NCCIH says that green tea as a beverage has no reported safety concerns for adults beyond its caffeine, whereas liver injury, though uncommon, has been reported mostly with extracts in tablet or capsule form, and that people with a certain immune-related gene variant, which it says 5 to 15 percent of Americans carry, appear especially susceptible. It also lists nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort and raised blood pressure as extract side effects [13].

EFSA reported that long-term intake of extracts above 800 mg EGCG per day raised liver enzymes in some people and that data were insufficient to set a safe dose; it considers traditionally prepared tea safe, with liver damage only rarely seen. Typical EU intake from tea is 90 to 300 mg of EGCG per day [1]. A 2020 Cochrane review listed gastrointestinal effects, raised liver enzymes and, less often, insomnia, raised blood pressure and skin reactions as possible adverse effects of extracts [1]. Green tea interferes with the cancer drug bortezomib and related proteasome inhibitors, and a 2024 review discusses possible interaction with alprazolam through CYP3A4 [1][4].

Wikipedia reports EFSA judged intakes of 338 mg per day from capsules and 704 mg per day from tea beverages as safe in a 2018 opinion, while 800 mg or more of EGCG per day could raise liver risk [19]. The NCCIH lists reduced blood levels of the beta-blocker nadolol with high doses, reduced atorvastatin levels with extract, and an interaction with raloxifene, and advises talking to a health care provider before supplements; caffeine intake in pregnancy should stay moderate [13].

Green tea sits at the border between food, supplement and cosmetic ingredient: brewed tea is a common beverage, extracts are supplements, and the extract is an ingredient in many creams and serums. Health Canada in 2017 recommended warning labels on extracts and use by adults only [1]. Beyond the wart ointment, no green tea product is approved in the US for a skin-appearance purpose [1][13].

Wikipedia summarizes randomized trials of green tea for non-appearance outcomes: small reductions in blood pressure (about 2 to 3 mm Hg), lower total and LDL cholesterol in a 2013 Cochrane meta-analysis, modest fasting-glucose effects with inconsistent results for HbA1c and insulin, no significant reduction in C-reactive protein in a 2015 meta-analysis, and no good evidence for weight loss [1]. A 2020 meta-analysis of cohort studies found no significant link between tea intake and colorectal cancer risk [8]. A randomized trial in people with knee osteoarthritis compared green tea with an active control [14], and a 2025 randomized trial examined green tea kombucha on oxidative stress and endothelial health in people with excess body weight [15].

For appearance, the evidence is mostly laboratory and in vivo antioxidant work on creams [3]. The one approved topical product, sinecatechins ointment, is for warts rather than for cosmetic purposes [11]. Registered studies of green tea examine oral lichen planus, xerostomia, gingivitis and plaque, lupus and prediabetes among others [16][17][18], none targeting skin ageing or body composition. EFSA found its skin-protection claims not sufficiently supported [1].

On T Nation, green tea extract appears in lifters' supplement lists alongside fish oil and fat-loss ingredients, and in discussions of leanness and general health [6][7]. Skincare communities treat it mainly as an antioxidant ingredient in serums and creams [3]. Matcha is discussed as a concentrated drinkable source of catechins, theanine and chlorophyll [5].

card.summary: Catechin-rich antioxidant botanical common in skincare; general health claims lack strong support and oral extracts carry liver warnings.
card.note: Oral extracts linked to liver toxicity; evidence here is from a single encyclopedia summary.

quick.overview:
Green tea extract concentrates the polyphenols of green tea leaf and is used in creams, serums and supplements as an antioxidant.

Reviews summarized on Wikipedia found insufficient evidence for most claims, though one topical form is an approved prescription for genital warts.
quick.mechanism: Catechins such as EGCG are antioxidants; no proven biological effects in humans are stated for them in the source.
quick.risks: Extracts, especially oral, have been linked to liver injury; EFSA could not set a safe dose. Rare skin reactions are reported.
